cf.title: Improve Hash/Merge Join estimate accuracy when all predicates are Hash/Merge clauses

input.subject: Improve Hash/Merge Join estimate accuracy when all predicates are Hash/Merge clauses

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and the goal of more accurate merge and hash join costs is not disputed. The open points are fixable: demand-1 asks for evidence that plan choice improves, standards-compat-1 asks whether the "stable" target means back-patching, and maintenance-fit-2 notes that nobody who knows selectivity estimation has judged the tradeoff in 0001. That tradeoff, raised in message #6 and accepted in message #7, needs a committer who knows the area.

brief.title: Use joinrel row estimate in merge/hash join costing; count NULLs in FK selectivity
brief.problem: final_cost_mergejoin() and final_cost_hashjoin() get mergejointuples/hashjointuples from approx_tuple_count(), which treats join clauses as independent. When the clauses match a multi-column FK, this underestimates the tuples passing the join quals, so the run cost is too low (5x in the author's example). Separately, FK-based join selectivity ignores NULLs in the referencing columns and can overestimate join size.
brief.proposed_design: 0002: for a JOIN_INNER join whose only join clauses are the merge/hash clauses, costing reuses path->jpath.path.rows instead of calling approx_tuple_count(). 0001: get_foreign_key_join_selectivity() scales the FK selectivity down by the table-wide null fraction of the referencing columns, using the largest per-column fraction for multi-column FKs. Columns with a strict restriction clause are skipped.
user_visible_surface: Merge and hash join run costs change in EXPLAIN output, which can change plan choice.
Join row estimates change for FK joins where referencing columns contain NULLs.
author_claims: The joinrel estimate is more accurate and free to reuse, since it comes from FK-aware clauselist_selectivity().
For JOIN_INNER only, path.rows equals the tuples passing the merge/hash quals; v1's two regressions came from semi and outer joins.
FK selectivity overestimates join size by 2x when half the referencing values are NULL; 0001 removes the XXX comment's two objections.
Taking the largest per-column null fraction is exact when FK columns are NULL together and a lower bound otherwise.
Regression tests are fragile here because only run costs change, which costs-off EXPLAIN does not show.
brief.thread_state: Xiangxin Zeng found an FK-with-NULLs case breaking v3, which led to 0001, then a case where 0001 underestimates because NULLs correlate with a filter on another column. The author accepts the tradeoff exists, and both ask for review from someone familiar with selfuncs.
unclear: Whether 0001's independence assumption between FK nullness and other filters is acceptable, or needs a narrower scope.
No benchmark shows plan changes or query time effects from either patch.
Which regression outputs v4 changes; v4 touches only costsize.c, and v1 changed several expected files.
How 0001 handles partly NULL multi-column FKs with MATCH SIMPLE beyond the lower-bound remark.
The CommitFest target is "stable", but the material does not say whether back-patching is intended.
search_queries: hash join cost estimate joinrel rows

objections.title: No real query shown where the cost change alters the chosen plan
objections.failure_scenario: After upgrade, a user with a stable workload sees some inner merge or hash joins switch to a different plan, because their run cost rose by cpu_tuple_cost per extra tuple. The material does not show whether these switches make queries faster or slower, so users find out from changed query times in production.
objections.argument: Every example in the thread is synthetic and turns off enable_hashjoin and enable_nestloop, so the plan never changes (messages #3, #4, #6). The 0002 delta in message #3 is 800 on a cost of about 10,900, and no benchmark shows that the change picks a better plan. 0002 applies to all plain inner merge and hash joins, so every user takes the risk of plan changes. Message #7 accepts that 0001 can underestimate when filters correlate with NULLs, which adds to that risk.
objections.author_must_show: Is there a real or benchmark workload, with planner settings left at their defaults, where either patch changes the chosen plan and the query time improves?

critic.reasoning: Every example in messages #3, #4 and #6 turns off enable_hashjoin and enable_nestloop, so none shows a plan change or a query time. The thread shows better cost accuracy only, and 0002 changes costs for all plain inner merge and hash joins.

objections.title: Target "stable" would ship planner estimate changes in minor releases
objections.failure_scenario: A site applies a minor update on a branch where 0001 was back-patched. A query with a filter correlated with FK nullness, as in message #6, has its join estimate halved. The planner then picks a nested loop or a different join order, and the site finds a slower query in production with no change of its own to explain it.
objections.argument: The CommitFest entry targets "stable", and nothing in the thread says whether back-patching is intended. Both patches change costs, and 0001 also changes join row estimates that feed every plan above the join. Message #7 accepts a known underestimate when NULLs correlate with a filter. Back branches normally avoid estimate changes that can flip plans without the user asking, so a committer would likely ask that the target be master only.
objections.author_must_show: Is this series meant for master only, and if not, why should known plan-changing estimate shifts go into minor releases?

critic.reasoning: The CommitFest entry says "Target version: stable" and no message says whether back-patching is intended. Message #7 accepts a known underestimate, so the question about minor releases stands, and a statement of master only would answer it.

objections.title: No one familiar with selectivity estimation has reviewed the FK change
objections.failure_scenario: 0001 is committed with its independence assumption between FK nullness and other filters. Users whose filters correlate with NULL FK values see join estimates halve, as in message #6, and get worse plans. The committer who pushed it owns these reports without an expert to judge whether the tradeoff was right.
objections.argument: Both participants ask for review from someone who knows selfuncs and cost estimation (messages #6, #7), and none has replied. The author agrees that 0001 swaps one assumption for another and that the scope may need to be narrower (message #7). FK-based join selectivity has been reverted before over bugs found after commit [P1], so changes in this function need an owner who knows the area.
objections.author_must_show: Has a committer who knows get_foreign_key_join_selectivity() reviewed whether the table-wide null fraction is an acceptable tradeoff against the case in message #6?

precedents.title: Revert "Use Foreign Key relationships to infer multi-column join selectivity".

critic.reasoning: Messages #6 and #7 both ask for review by someone who knows selfuncs, and no such reply is shown. P1 must not be used as support, because it records bugs in the first FK selectivity implementation, which do not bear on this change.

refuted.title: Cost invariant in 0002 has no test that would catch a break
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how joinrestrictinfo or the JOIN_INNER joinrel row count is built, so path.rows no longer equals the tuples passing the merge/hash quals. Merge and hash join run costs drift and plans change. No regression test fails, so users find it later as plan regressions in a release.
refuted.argument: 0002 rests on an unstated equality between path.rows and the tuples passing the merge/hash quals. v1 already broke this equality for semi and outer joins without any loud failure (messages #1, #2). The author says regression tests are fragile because costs-off EXPLAIN hides run costs (message #5), and v4 touches only costsize.c. So nothing in the tree would flag the next break. A committer would likely ask for an assertion or a cost-visible test before taking on this coupling.
refuted.author_must_show: What test or assertion would fail if a future change made path.rows differ from the tuples passing the merge/hash quals for an inner join?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on an unnamed future patch, and a drift would be a less accurate cost estimate, which approx_tuple_count() already is. v1's semi and outer join cases did show up, in changed regression output and in the author's table in message #1.

refuted.title: Target version "stable" for changes that alter plan choice
refuted.failure_scenario: If both patches are back-patched, users on a minor release see new join row estimates and merge/hash costs. Some queries switch plans after a minor upgrade with no change on their side. They find out when a production query slows down after routine patching.
refuted.argument: The CommitFest entry targets "stable", but the thread does not say whether back-patching is intended. Both patches change estimates and costs that drive plan choice, and message #6 shows 0001 makes at least one estimate worse than master. The project usually keeps planner estimate changes out of minor releases to keep plans stable. No benchmark in the thread shows the size of plan changes.
refuted.author_must_show: Is back-patching intended, and if so, what makes these estimate changes safe to ship in a minor release?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same back-patching concern with a more concrete scenario.

questions: Is there a workload, with planner settings at their defaults, where either patch changes the chosen plan and the query time improves?
Is the series meant for master only, and if not, why should plan-changing estimate shifts go into minor releases?
Should 0001 apply only when the referencing rel has no restriction clauses, given the underestimate shown in message #6?
Which regression outputs change with v4, given that v1 changed several expected files and v4 touches only costsize.c?
With MATCH SIMPLE and partly NULL multi-column FKs, how far can the largest per-column null fraction be from the true fraction of non-matching rows?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows join selectivity estimation and costsize.c, in particular get_foreign_key_join_selectivity() and the merge and hash join cost functions.
committability.liability: The owner signs for plan changes on every plain inner merge or hash join, and for FK join estimates that drop when NULLs correlate with a filter. Reports can arrive for as long as the estimates stay in the planner.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted four versions and answered the reviewer's cases in the thread, with a new patch for the first one. The thread was idle for over a year between message #1 and message #2.

priority.reason: Multi-column and nullable FK joins are common, and both patches are small and touch only costsize.c. Both participants ask for review by someone who knows selfuncs, and none has replied; review cost is set to medium because no code was read.

provisional_note: Without the code, the review could not check that 0002's condition matches exactly the joins whose only join clauses are the merge or hash clauses. It also could not check how 0001 detects strict restriction clauses and combines null fractions.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 137805f89 as well as the associated commits 015e88942,
5306df283, and 68d704edb.  We found multiple bugs in this feature, and
there was concern about possible planner slowdown (though to be fair,
exhibiting a very large slowdown proved difficult).  The way forward
requires a considerable rewrite, which may or may not be possible to
accomplish in time for beta2.  In my judgment reviewing the rewrite will
be easier to accomplish starting from a clean slate, so let's temporarily
revert what's there now.  This also leaves us in a safe state if it turns
out to be necessary to postpone the rewrite to the next development cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve join selectivity estimation using extended statistics
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses per-table extended statistics, mainly functional dependencies, when it estimates join selectivity in clausesel.c. It also tries to combine join clauses with relation-level filters in calc_joinrel_size_estimate to estimate conditional probabilities.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra found the design at the wrong level of abstraction. Clausesel.c handled extended statistics directly, dependencies were applied clause by clause in a fixed order and only on the inner relation, and he proposed handling all join clauses for a pair of relations at once in extended_stats.c. The author agreed it could be done better but posted no new version. In July the patch no longer compiled, and it still did not one commitfest later, so it was returned with feedback.
matched_queries: hash join cost estimate joinrel rows
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The patch includes some *very* interesting ideas, but I think it's does them too late and at the wrong level of abstraction.

precedents_retrieved.title: improving join estimates using FK
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner use foreign keys between joined tables to estimate join selectivity, so a multi-column join that matches a foreign key gets an estimate of about 1/N of the referenced table. Later versions also tried to find foreign keys through equivalence classes and to handle joins of more than two relations.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was closed because the author did not post a new version after David Rowley's revised patch, which was waiting for the author's review. Open design problems remained: with several relations on one side of the join, the same foreign key can match more than once, and taking the minimum selectivity was a known approximation. Also, the referenced rows may not all be present in a joined relation.
matched_queries: hash join cost estimate joinrel rows
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Tomas, I think we need you need to submit a new version of this patch, please.  Closing it for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Using multicolumn statistics for more precise join selectivity estimatation
precedents_retrieved.objectors: vignesh C, Yugo NAGATA, Tomas Vondra
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch had two parts. One let the planner use extended (multicolumn) statistics, specifically functional dependencies, when estimating join selectivity. The other made auto_explain create multicolumn statistics automatically, or just suggest them, when a plan node's estimated row count differs from the actual count by more than a threshold.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last visible message (July 2021) reports that the patch no longer compiled on Windows against changed ModifyTableState fields. The same message says Yugo Nagata's open review comments still needed addressing, and the entry was moved to Waiting on Author. Those comments included duplicate statistics suggestions causing a unique-constraint error, redundant suggestions, and a request to explain why each statistic is suggested. Earlier, Tomas Vondra had suggested moving the advisor into a separate extension rather than auto_explain, collecting data across many runs, and not creating statistics automatically. The visible messages show no new version after that, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also Yugo Nagata's comments need to be addressed, I'm changing the
status to "Waiting for Author".

precedents_retrieved.title: Patch to implement missing join selectivity estimation for range types
precedents_retrieved.authors: Mahmoud SAKR (mahmsakr), Diogo Repas (diogo.repas), Maxime Schoemans (mschoema), Zhicheng Luo (zcsysu.163.com)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, vignesh C, jian he, Tomas Vondra
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds join selectivity estimation for range and multirange operators such as <<, >>, &&, &<, &>, @> and <@, using the existing bounds histograms instead of the constant 0.005. A multirange is treated as its bounding range.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After the January 2024 revision, the CFBot still showed an AddressSanitizer abort in calc_hist_join_selectivity, and the authors did not post a fix. The function was still duplicated in rangetypes_selfuncs.c and multirangetypes_selfuncs.c, which Tomas Vondra, Tom Lane and jian he asked to remove. jian he also asked for estimate-ratio tests in place of the 3-way join plans, and the thread ends with no reply from the authors.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I also agree with the upthread criticism that having two identical functions in different source files will be a maintenance nightmare.

precedents_retrieved.title: estimating joins using extended statistics
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses multi-column MCV lists from extended statistics to estimate equijoin selectivity, matching the MCV lists of the two joined relations the way eqjoinsel_inner does. It can also use base restrictions as conditions on the MCV lists, and estimates joins of more than two relations one relation pair at a time.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer objected to the design in the visible messages. The last messages report that the 2022-01-01 version fails cfbot with uninitialized-variable warnings in mcv_combine_simple() and no longer applies to master, and no new version appears before the entry was returned. The author still listed open items, such as no support for outer or inequality joins and possibly wrong ndistinct and nullfract assumptions for column subsets.
matched_queries: hash join cost estimate joinrel rows
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Also the patch doesn't apply anymore:

precedents_retrieved.title: PoC: improving join estimates using sampling
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a "sample" kind to create statistics, so the planner samples tables during planning to estimate scan and join selectivity. Joins on a primary key use correlated sampling: the planner samples the table without the key randomly and looks up the matching rows in the other table.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Planning overhead was too high: the two-table example took about 600 ms to plan. The planner sampled the same relation several times, and the correlated sample ran one SPI lookup per row. Andres Freund noted the PoC had not been updated since January and was in the final CF, and he said the planner first needs a way to tell cheap plans from expensive ones so it samples only when useful. Tomas Vondra agreed it should be moved or returned, and that sampling would stay too expensive for simple queries.
matched_queries: hash join cost estimate joinrel rows
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But even if we manage to make this much cheaper, there will still be
simple queries where it's going to be prohibitively expensive.

precedents_retrieved.title: Select Reference Page - Make Join Syntax More Prominent
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch reworks the SELECT reference page so that join syntax is more prominent, adding a separate recursive join_expression element to the FROM clause synopsis. It also moves the LATERAL description above the join parameters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that describing from_item as disjoint from join_expression is wrong and would confuse readers. He proposed adding introductory text to the "FROM Clause" section and keeping LATERAL last. The author disagreed but said he would do another pass, and the visible messages show no revised patch before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think it's fundamentally wrong to
describe from_item as disjoint from join_expression, and you're
going to make people more confused not less so by doing that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow foreign keys to reference a superset of unique columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: Allow a foreign key constraint to reference a set of columns that is a superset of the columns of a non-deferrable unique or primary key index on the referenced table, rather than requiring an exact match. An optional USING INDEX clause after the referenced column list would name the supporting unique index where the choice would otherwise be ambiguous.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the semantics are questionable (for example CASCADE behaviour of the extra columns, nullable subset columns, MATCH PARTIAL and UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT), that the change could break existing optimizations, and that it risks conflict with the SQL standard and its information_schema. He said a patch was premature unless the SQL committee standardized the behaviour. Peter Eisentraut said that working out the full specification was the open work still required of the proposal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think the semantics are at best questionable, I think
it will break important optimizations, and I think the chances of
finding ourselves in conflict with some future SQL spec extension are
too high.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent is the same idea, and none has a recorded reason that applies here. [P1] and [P3] built the FK-based join estimate that 0001 adjusts, but they ended over bugs, planner slowdown and a stalled revision. [P2] used extended statistics at the wrong abstraction level, and [P18] has no recorded reason. Inside the thread, the only earlier decision is the XXX comment in get_foreign_key_join_selectivity(). The 0001 commit message says it handles both of that comment's reasons, and message #6 raises a different issue, the correlation between nullness and filters, which belongs to the design angle.
The proposal adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or psql change, so it has no pg_dump, standard or client surface. The only objection from this angle concerns the "stable" target.

Both patches change only planner cost and row estimates in costsize.c. They add no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog column, wire protocol message or extension-visible struct, so pg_upgrade, standbys, subscribers and mixed-version clusters are not affected. The CommitFest target is "stable", which would mean plan changes in a minor release, but that is a planner-behaviour question for another angle and the material does not say back-patching is intended.

The proposal changes planner cost and row estimates only: merge/hash join run costs and FK join selectivity from existing pg_statistic null fractions. It adds no privilege, object, function, GUC, view or connection path, and exposes no statistics beyond what EXPLAIN already shows, so the security angle has no objection.

Postgres has no existing feature, option or extension that corrects the merge/hash join run cost or the NULL-blind FK selectivity, and both patches extend existing estimator code rather than adding a second mechanism. Whether 0001's independence assumption is acceptable is a design question for the selfuncs angle, outside this one.
Multi-column and nullable FK joins are common, so the underlying estimation problem is plausible. The only demand gap is evidence that the cost change helps real plan choices.
